questions.question: Explain why trekboers moved into the interior in the eighteenth century.
questions.expected_answer: Large families meant sons needed land; good land near Cape Town was taken and expensive; stock farming was cheap to start and livestock could walk to market; the loan farm system (1714) gave large farms for a small fee; desire to escape Company control, taxes and fixed prices; grazing, game and opportunities to obtain Khoikhoi cattle.

questions.question: Describe the lifestyle of the trekboers.
questions.expected_answer: Semi-nomadic; lived in ox wagons, tents or simple clay/wattle-and-daub houses; wealth in sheep, cattle, goats and horses; hunted game; small gardens; self-sufficient - made soap, candles, leather riems and veldskoene; travelled rarely to Cape Town, Swellendam or Graaff-Reinet to sell butter, soap, hides and livestock and buy guns, gunpowder, coffee, sugar, tea, cloth and tools; Bible-centred religion; limited schooling (meesters); independent, family-loyal, suspicious of government.

questions.question: How did trekboer expansion affect the Khoikhoi and San?
questions.expected_answer: Khoikhoi lost grazing land, water and cattle; many became servants (herders, drivers, guides) for food and shelter, tied by debt and the indenture of children (inboekstelsel from 1775, to age 25). The San lost hunting grounds and game, resisted from the 1770s by raiding, and were attacked by commandos that killed thousands and captured children - genocidal violence that destroyed many San communities by 1800.
